title_r: Reproduction Package for FSE 2024 Submission `A Replication Study of Interpolation-Based Hardware Model Checking for Software Verification'
abstract_r:
Reproduction Package A Replication Study of Interpolation-Based Hardware Model Checking for Software Verification Abstract This artifact is a reproduction package for the manuscript “A Replication Study of Interpolation-Based Hardware Model Checking for Software Verification”, submitted to FSE 2024. In the replication study, the transferability of the results reported by two prior publications on interpolation-based hardware model checking to software verification is investigated. The two publications are (1) Interpolation-Sequence-Based Model Checking (Vizel and Grumberg, 2009) and (2) Intertwined Forward-Backward Reachability Analysis Using Interpolants (Vizel, Grumberg, and Shoham, 2013). The purpose of this artifact is to reproduce the experiments conducted to validate the claims made in the above two publications. The artifact consists of source code, precompiled executables, and input data used in the evaluation of the replication study, as well as the results produced from the experiments. Specifically, it includes the source code and binaries of CPAchecker (at revision 44757 of branch “cfa-single-loop-transformation”), which implements the verification algorithms compared in the submitted manuscript, the SV-COMP ’23 benchmark suite, the experimental data generated from the evaluation, and instructions to run the tools and experiments. This reproduction package works best with the SoSy-Lab Virtual Machine, which runs Ubuntu 22.04 LTS. The VM has all the required dependencies installed. If you test this artifact with it, all installation steps below can be skipped. Contents This artifact contains the following items: README.*: this documentation fse2024-paper483.pdf: the manuscript submitted to FSE 2024 License.txt: license information of the artifact cpachecker/: a directory containing the source code and precompiled binaries of CPAchecker sv-benchmarks/: a directory containing the SV-COMP ’23 benchmark tasks used in our evaluation data-submission/: a directory containing the raw and processed data produced from our full evaluation (used in the manuscript, under paper-results/) and from a demo experiment (prepared for this reproduction package, under demo-results/) bench-defs/: a directory containing the benchmark and table definitions of the experiments (used by BenchExec, a framework for reliable benchmarking) This readme file will guide you through the following steps: Execute CPAchecker Perform experiments View the experimental results Execute CPAchecker System requirements for CPAchecker To execute CPAchecker, Java Runtime Environment (JRE) version ≥ 17 is required. For more information, please refer to cpachecker/INSTALL.md. Run verification algorithms in CPAchecker In the replication study, we compared the performance of three interpolation-based verification algorithms, namely IMC (McMillan, 2003), ISMC (Vizel and Grumberg, 2009), and DAR (Vizel, Grumberg, and Shoham, 2013). ISMC and DAR are the algorithms proposed by the two prior publications, respectively, and IMC is the first interpolation-based model-checking approach, which was used as the baseline in the two publications. All the algorithms have been implemented in CPAchecker. Below we list the commands to run the evaluated verification algorithms. These example commands use sv-benchmarks/c/loop-invariants/even.c as the input program. You can replace it with another program. IMC: 
# expected verification result: TRUE cpachecker/scripts/cpa.sh -32 -spec sv-comp-reachability \ -bmc-interpolation \ -setprop cpa.predicate.memoryAllocationsAlwaysSucceed=true \ -setprop cpa.predicate.refinement.verifyInterpolants=true \ -setprop cfa.transformIntoSingleLoop=true \ -setprop imc.fallBack=false \ -setprop imc.loopBoundIncrementStrategyForBMC=CONST \ sv-benchmarks/c/loop-invariants/even.c
ISMC: 
# expected verification result: TRUE cpachecker/scripts/cpa.sh -32 -spec sv-comp-reachability \ -bmc-interpolationSequence \ -setprop cpa.predicate.memoryAllocationsAlwaysSucceed=true \ -setprop cpa.predicate.refinement.verifyInterpolants=true \ -setprop cfa.transformIntoSingleLoop=true \ -setprop imc.fallBack=false \ sv-benchmarks/c/loop-invariants/even.c
DAR: 
# expected verification result: TRUE cpachecker/scripts/cpa.sh -32 -spec sv-comp-reachability \ -bmc-interpolationDualSequence \ -setprop cpa.predicate.memoryAllocationsAlwaysSucceed=true \ -setprop cpa.predicate.refinement.verifyInterpolants=true \ -setprop cfa.transformIntoSingleLoop=true \ -setprop dar.fallBack=false \ sv-benchmarks/c/loop-invariants/even.c
For more information on how to run CPAchecker, see cpachcker/README.md. Understand the output of CPAchecker The following is an example output shown on the console after an analysis is finished. 
[...redacted...] Verification result: TRUE. No property violation found by chosen configuration. More details about the verification run can be found in the directory "./output". Graphical representation included in the file "./output/Report.html".
There are 3 possible outcomes of the verification result: TRUE: the program is “safe”, i.e., it satisfies the given safety property FALSE: the program is “unsafe”, i.e., it contains a violation to the given safety property UNKNOWN: the analysis was inconclusive CPAchecker also generates an HTML report for conveniently browsing the results. Please refer to cpachecker/doc/Report.md for more information. Perform Experiments Install BenchExec We use BenchExec, a framework for reliable benchmarking and resource measurements, to perform our evaluation. Please follow the installation guide to set up the benchmarking environment. Experimental settings The settings are described in the XML file bench-defs/cpachecker-slt.xml. This XML file is used by BenchExec for limiting computing resources and scheduling runs. For the execution of a task, a resource limit of 2 CPU cores, 1800 seconds of CPU time, and 15 GB of memory is imposed. Run the Full Evaluation To run the full experiment over the 8813 benchmark tasks reported in the manuscript, execute the following command. 
benchexec bench-defs/cpachecker-slt.xml \ --tool-directory cpachecker/ -o results/ \ --read-only-dir / --overlay-dir . --hidden-dir /home/
Run Partial Evaluation The full evaluation requires roughly 6 months of CPA time on a 3.40 GHz core. To run the experiment on a subset of benchmark tasks, you could add -t <tasks_name> to the above command, where <task_name> refer to the task names defined in bench-defs/cpachecker-slt.xml. For example: 
benchexec bench-defs/cpachecker-slt.xml \ --tool-directory cpachecker/ -o results/ \ --read-only-dir / --overlay-dir . --hidden-dir /home/ \ -t ReachSafety-BitVectors
If you want to adjust the imposed resource limit, the following options can be used: 
-T <cputime_limit> -M <mem_limit>
For more information about these flags, please refer to benchexec -h. View the Experimental Results Generate Tables After the execution of an experiment, you can generate an interactive HTML by table-generator. Simply run: 
table-generator -x bench-defs/overall-slt-stats.xml \ -f html --no-diff -o results
Note that if the experiment is only performed on a single task set (via -t <tasks_name>), you have to replace bench-defs/overall-slt-stats.xml by bench-defs/subset-slt-stats.xml. Results from Our Experiments The results (both raw and processed data) of the partial run (on ReachSafety-BitVectors) and the full run obtained by our machines are in folders data-submission/demo-results/ and data-submission/paper-results/, respectively. The generated HTML tables are named overall-slt-stats.table.html under each respective folder. In the replication study, there are eight hypotheses extracted from the two prior publications. We list them below to make this document more standalone. For details, please refer to the bundled manuscript. Claims in the ISMC Publication H1.A: ISMC is faster than IMC on tasks with property violation. H1.B: ISMC is faster than IMC when IMC finds a proof only at high unrolling bounds. H1.C: Overall, ISMC is faster than IMC (by 30 % in this experiment). In our experiments, we confirmed H1.A also for software verification, but H1.B and H1.C did not hold. Claims in the DAR Publication H2.A: For DAR, the ratio between iterations using global strengthening to the total number of iterations is less than 0.5 in most tasks. H2.B: IMC finds a proof slower than DAR in many tasks even though it has a smaller convergence length. H2.C: DAR computes more interpolants than IMC. H2.D: DAR’s run-time is more sensitive to the sizes of interpolants than IMC. H2.E: Overall, DAR is faster than IMC (by 36 % in this experiment). In our experiments, we confirmed H2.A and H2.C also for software verification, but H2.B, H2.D, and H2.E did not hold. Flaherty and Ragnhild Balsvik, published in: Journal of Comments and Replications in Economics, Volume 2, 2023-3. Abstract: This paper replicates Poole (2013) using comprehensive Norwegian and Irish register data. abstract_r:

Vieider [(2009). The effect of accountability on loss aversion. Acta Psychologica, 132(1), 96–101.] reported that this irrational tendency to avoid losses can be reduced by holding people accountable. The present study initially aimed to clarify whether this effect is driven by either process or outcome accountability. However, as we did not find any effects of either process or outcome accountability on loss aversion in two experiments, our focus shifted towards a direct replication attempt. Our third experiment used materials, procedures, and manipulations that closely matched those of the original study, and almost doubled its sample size. Despite these efforts, we still did not replicate Vieider's findings, with a Bayesian test providing substantial evidence in favor of the null hypothesis of no difference between experimental conditions.

item37: Firstly, the participant demographics in the replication study was different as compared to the original study. Our current study’s participants had a much smaller sample size in the current study (32 participants in our current study and 169 participants in the original study), and an average age that was almost 10 years younger than that of the original study, with twice the number of people being unemployed at the point of testing as compared to the original study. These differences could have contributed to our inability to replicate the findings of the original study, as the younger age group and differential employment status of participants in the current study could mean that they might have different types of thinking from participants in the original study, thus affecting their ratings of the perceived typicality of the situation.
Secondly, there is no compensation provided to participants, and this could have affected their motivation to pay attention to the items in the study, resulting in inattentiveness in their responses, that might not have been detected by the manipulation check questions. Singer (2002) found that monetary incentives can be used to motivate participation in individuals, and the authors of the original study (Motro & Ellis, 2017) similarly provided participants with monetary compensation should they be included in their data set. 
Thirdly, the fact that employee Pat shown in the video to participants was a White individual, it could have influenced the perceived psychological realism of the participants of our current study, as they are all Asians, and might have difficulty relating to the situation shown as Pat is of a different ethnicity.  Additionally, in this replication study, the participants were not told to imagine that they were the direct supervisor of Pat, the employee in the video, unlike in the original study as the researchers had deduced it was necessary only for the second hypothesis which was not replicated. Both of these factors might have lessened the psychological realism created for the participants in the present replication, which could have contributed to the non-significant finding.

title_r: Replication and Extension of Nozaradan, Peretz, Missal and Mouraux (2011)
abstract_r: Frequency tagging has been used to capture auditory entrainment to beat and meter in music. Specifically, Nozaradan, Peretz, Missal and Mouraux (2011) instructed listeners to imagine either a binary or ternary metrical pattern while listening to an isochronous auditory stimulus and recorded cortical responses using electroencephalography (EEG). The amplitude of brain activity was increased at beat-related frequencies in both imagery conditions. This study inspired other labs to use the frequency tagging approach to examine auditory rhythm perception, and in only 6 years, it has been cited over 250 times on Google Scholar. The frequency tagging technique has been used in several published papers since 2011 and it is being used increasingly in research presented at recent research conferences and symposia. However, this seminal study has not been replicated. This registered report will detail the results of multiple independent conceptual replications of Nozaradan et al. (2011), all of which will follow the same vetted protocol.

title_r: The effect of selective spatial attention on the development of secondary hyperalgesia: a replication study
abstract_r: Cognitive factors, such as attention, play an important role in the modulation of pain and in the development of pain chronicity. We attempt to replicate one such effect found in a previous study conducted by Filbrich et al., 2020, which shows how the experimental induction of central sensitization, a key factor in the development of secondary hyperalgesia, can indeed be modulated by selective spatial attention. Secondary hyperalgesia occurs after tissue injury. It refers to a condition of increased sensitivity to mechanical stimuli within the injured area and the surrounding skin. It is hypothesized that the intense and sustained activation of peripheral nociceptors enhances the responsiveness of the neurons in the central nervous system. This causes the phenomenon known as central sensitization which is considered to play a key role in the development of chronic pain. As in Filbrich (2020), we will manipulate the impact of selective spatial attention by asking healthy volunteers to selectively focus their attention on target stimuli applied on one of the two forearms while we apply high frequency stimulation on both forearms. To assess the effect of the manipulation, we will measure perceived intensity to mechanical pinprick stimuli on both arms at three different moments: at T0, before applying high-frequency stimulation (HFS), at T1, immediately after having applied HFS in combination with the selective attention task, and finally at T2, 20 minutes after the whole procedure. Moreover, at T2, we will estimate the extent of the area of secondary hyperalgesia on both arms by applying mechanical pinprick stimulation along two axes: (1) medial-later, and (2) proximal-distal. title_r: GW4 21-22: Devaluation effects in food-specific response inhibition training: An independent conceptual replication
abstract_r:
OSF registration template: Open-Ended Registration

Food-specific inhibitory control training (F-ICT) is a behavioural intervention in which participants learn to associate certain food-types with the inhibition of behaviour. Research has demonstrated the effectiveness of such training in reducing food evaluations (e.g., Chen et al., 2016; Chen, Veling, de Vries, et al., 2018; Veling et al., 2013a), changing food choices (e.g., Veling et al., 2013b; Veling, Chen, et al., 2017), decreasing food intake (e.g., Lawrence, Verbruggen, et al., 2015; also see Allom et al., 2016) and even promoting weight loss (Lawrence, O’Sullivan, et al., 2015; Nederkoorn et al., 2010; Veling et al., 2014; see Jones et al., 2016 for a meta-analysis). This has led some researchers to suggest that F-ICT may be a cost-effective intervention with clinical utility (Carbine & Larson, 2019; Jones et al., 2016, 2018). 

One explanation for the effectiveness of F-ICT on health-related outcomes is provided by the Behaviour Stimulus Interaction (BSI) theory (Chen et al., 2016; Veling et al., 2008; Veling, Lawrence, et al., 2017), which proposes that during training food stimuli are devalued to reduce the response conflict caused by the need to inhibit motor responses towards (highly) appetitive items and thus facilitate task performance. In a series of six experiments using the Go/No-Go Task, Chen et al. (2016) examined the effect of of food-specific response inhibition training on stimulus devaluation by pairing appetitive stimuli with cues to respond (go stimuli) or with cues to not respond (no-go cues or the absence of cues). Providing evidence of stimulus devaluation, findings indicated that attractiveness ratings of no-go foods reduced after training whilst ratings of go-foods increased. This effect was then replicated in two preregistered experiments (Chen, Veling, Dijksterhuis, et al., 2018) and across obese and normal-weight individuals (Chen, Veling, de Vries, et al., 2018), showing consistently that no-go foods were rated as less attractive post-training compared to go-foods and untrained foods.

title_r: Self Regulation Ontology Replication
abstract_r:
OSF registration template: Open-Ended Registration

summary: Previously (Eisenberg et al., 2019), our lab leveraged exploratory factor analysis (EFA) on the dependent variables (n=193 DVs) extracted from 522 individuals’ performances on a large range of tasks (n=37 tasks, n=129 DVs) and self-report surveys (n=22 surveys, n=64 DVs) broadly related to the psychological construct of ‘Self Regulation’. While 12 factors were recovered from the survey DVs, only 5 factors were recovered from task-derived DVs. of the 5 task factors, 3 (speeded information processing, caution, and perception/response) were strongly related to DVs that were parameters of drift diffusion modeling (DDM): drift rate, threshold, and non-decision time, respectively. This may indicate that DDM captures fundamental dimensions of cognition. Alternative, this could suggest that examining the data through the lens of DDM conceals otherwise fundamental cognitive factors that are central to other taxonomies in the literature (e.g., Miyake et al., 2000), like shifting, updating, and inhibition. 
	To investigate these possibilities, we plan to perform EFA and the subsequent analyses of Eisenberg et al. (2019) on the original data, replacing the DDM parameters with reaction time, accuracy, and within-subject reaction time standard deviation. We propose two competing hypothesis classes.  First, the factors recovered could be similar in number and occupy a similar factor space and axes as the original factors. For example, we could again find a 5-factor solution, but dependent variables that previously loaded on speeded information processing, caution, and perception/response may now load onto RT variance, accuracy, and mean reaction time, respectively. Within this class, a more specific outcome would be that these new factors provide worse fits to the data than the original factors. This would indicate that the additional assumptions of the DDM combined with the original modeling parameters produce dependent variables which better reflect the underlying psychological factor space. Alternatively, the new factors could better fit the data compared to the old factors, indicating that the additional assumptions of DDM distort the data in some way, and would encourage further investigation. 
	Second, the new factor solution may be fundamentally different in factor number and factor space/axes. For example, the original 5-factor solution may give way to a higher-dimensional solution in which dependent variables map onto more traditional psychological constructs like attention, working memory, shifting, inhibition, etc.  Alternatively, we may recover a set of factors more obscure that do not map cleanly onto the original factor solution or existing taxonomies of cognitive processes (e.g., Miyake et al., 2000). 
	The first class of hypotheses would provide evidence that the Eisenberg et al. (2019) ontology is robust to the presence or absence of the DDM modeling and transformation of the raw reaction and accuracy data. Alternatively, the second class of hypotheses would suggest that the ontology (Eisenberg et al., 2019) is more idiosyncratic to analytical decisions like whether to analyze the data through the lens of the DDM.

item29: 1.	Verbal description of the effect I am trying to replicate (optional)  The study “The dark triad and honesty rules in romantic relationships” by Muñoz and De Los Reyes (2021) examined the connection between the three traits of the dark triad (i.e., Psychopathy, Machiavellianism and Narcissism) and honesty rule endorsement in romantic relationships, defined as obligatory rules and discretionary rules. Obligatory rules consist of strict standards for honest communication, while discretionary rules provide the flexibility to determine when deception is appropriate. We are trying to replicate the following hypotheses:  1.	High Psychopathy positively predicts discretionary rule endorsement.  2.	High Psychopathy negatively predicts obligatory rule endorsement.  3.	High Machiavellianism positively predicts discretionary rule endorsement. 4.	Narcissism shows no effects on either honesty rule endorsement.   2.	It is important to replicate this effect because (optional)  With the replication crisis in mind, it is important to strengthen the confidence in the reliability of the reported effects, so that this replication study should promote the confidence in the postulated relationships between the dark triad traits and honesty rule endorsement (Brandt, 2014).  Further, in the original study, 98.05% of the participants were Hispanics and most of the participants were female. Thus, this replication study which will be conducted with a German sample and a more balanced gender ratio will help to answer the question concerning the generalizability of the findings of the original study to other contexts.   3.	The effect size of the effect I am trying to replicate is (optional)  1.	The effect size of the effect between psychopathy and discretionary rule endorsement is r = .26.  2.	The effect size of the effect between psychopathy and obligatory rule endorsement is r = -.10. This effect is mentioned as significant in the text but not in the attached bivariate correlation matrix.  3.	The effect size of the effect between Machiavellianism and discretionary rule endorsement is r = .28.  4.	The confidence interval of the original effect is (optional)  Not specified   5.	The sample size of the original effect is (optional)  Two different sample sizes are reported in the paper. According to the text, the sample size is N = 257, but according to the bivariate correlation matrix, the sample size is N = 258.    6.	Where was the original study conducted? (e.g., lab, in the field, online) (optional)  The original study was conducted online.   7.	What country/region was the original study conducted in? (optional)  The researchers are from University of Texas, but it is not clear in the text where the study was conducted in.  8.	What kind of sample did the original study use? (e.g. student, Mturk, representative) (optional)  The original sample consisted of n = 221 females, n = 35 males, n = 1 or 2 other (see Point 5). 95.33% of the participants were between 18 and 29 years old and 98.05% self-identified as Hispanic. No further information were given.  9.	Was the original study conducted with paper-and-pencil surveys, on a computer, or something else? (optional)  The original study was conducted on a computer.    Designing the Replication Study  10.	Are the original materials for the study available from the author? (optional)  -	No  11.	I know that assumptions (e.g., about the meaning of the stimuli) in the original study will also hold in my replication because (optional)  We will use validated and empirically tested questionnaires. For the assessment of the Dark Triad character traits, we will use the Short Dark Triad (SD3; Jones & Paulhus, 2014) which includes 9 items each for Machiavellianism, Narcissism and Psychopathy. It was already translated to German so we will use the translated version (Malesza et al., 2017). The other questionnaire we will use is a measure of honesty rules endorsement in relationships which includes 21 obligatory rule statements and 22 discretionary rule statements (Roggensack & Sillars, 2014). This questionnaire is written in English, so we will translate it to German. The translations will be checked by an English native speaker. By that we will make sure that the original meaning will not be distorted. For both questionnaires we will use a 5-point Likert-type scale (strongly disagree to strongly agree). We will also ask for participants age, culture and gender to rule out any impact on the effect.  12.	Location of the experimenter during data collection (optional)  Not applicable   13.	Experimenter knowledge of participant experimental condition (optional)  Not applicable   14.	Experimenter knowledge of overall hypotheses (optional)  All experimenters know about all hypotheses.   15.	My target sample size is (optional)  Our target sample size is N = 256, but we will collect N = 270 participants because of possible exclusions.  16.	The rationale for my sample size is (optional)  An a priori power analysis for correlation was conducted, assuming an effect size of r = .26 (which was smallest significant effect reported in the original study), setting Type I error rate at  = .05 and power at 99%. The similarities/differences in the measures are (optional)  -	Close   19.	The similarities/differences in the stimuli are (optional)  Not applicable   20.	The similarities/differences in the location (e.g., lab vs. online; alone vs. in groups) are (optional)  -	Exact  21.	The similarities/differences in remuneration are (optional)  The remuneration is not given in the paper. There will be no remuneration in our replication.   22.	The similarities/differences between participant populations are (optional)  -	Close   23.	What differences between the original study and your study might be expected to influence the size and/or direction of the effect? (optional)  Because we do not have the original materials there might be differences in the instruction text of the study and as already mentioned (see Point 11), we will self-translate the English questionnaire for honesty rules endorsement in relationships to German.   24.	I have taken the following steps to test whether the differences listed in the previous question will influence the outcome of my replication attempt (optional)  The translations will be checked by an English native speaker. By that we will make sure that the original meaning will not be distorted (see Point 11).  Analysis and Replication Evaluation  25.	My exclusion criteria are (e.g., handling outliers, removing participants from analysis) (optional)  We will exclude participants who don’t give their consent to participate and those who are younger than 18 years. If participants answer one of the attention check questions incorrectly, participants will be excluded afterwards.   26.	My analysis plan is (justify differences from the original) (optional)  First we will calculate descriptive statistics for all relevant variables (i.e, Machiavellianism, Psychopathy, Narcissism, obligatory rule endorsement and discretionary rule endorsement). Then, we will calculate an intercorrelation matrix for all relevant variables. Lastly, we will conduct two regression analyses with each trait of the dark triad as the predictor for obligatory rule endorsement and discretionary rule endorsement as dependent variables.   27. title_r: Will humans obey authority even though it can risk anothers life? A direct replication of the Milgram study.
abstract_r: One of the most famous studies in social psychology was completed by Stanley Milgram. Milgram's experiment's primary focus was on the conflict between obedience to authority and conscience of the participants (Milgram, 1963). Milgram was specifically interested in actions completed under World War II - can the horrible acts of nazi soldiers be explained with that they were only following orders from authorities? The procedure was that the participant was paired with one of Milgram´s confederates. The experiment conducted two roles - teacher and learner, the real participant was always the teacher. The learner was placed in a room and had electrodes attached to his arms. The teacher and researcher stayed in a room next door. Teacher´s room contained an electric shock generator and switches marked from 15 volts and up to 450 volts. The teacher was supposed to administer an electric shock every time the learner made a mistake, and also increase the level of the shock each time the answer was wrong. The experimenter also played an active role in the experiment and encouraged the teacher to continue to press on the switch, even though the learner protested. At the end of the experiment 65% of the participants continued to the 450 volts and all of the participants continued to 300 volts (Milgram, 1963). Milligrams' explanation about the findings was that the circumstances had such a big influence on the participants. With that in consideration the aspects of the situation such as the location, the behavior of the experimenter (authority) and the fact that the participants got paid could potentially change the behavior of the participants. But it is clear that people are more likely to follow orders given by authority. Milgram concluded that our aspects of moral and obedience carry enormous importance, but unfortunately those factors say little about how people will behave in different situations (Milgram, 1963). It has been many years since Milgram's experiment was completed. People's beliefs and attitudes have been through a dramatic change. Yet, it is important to replicate the study to see if those changes in our society have any kind of impact on the situations where participants may or may not agree to things that they find unpleasant. Another key question that should be answered by replicating this study is - are people still willing to harm others in pursuit of obeying authority? We found it important to replicate Millgram´s study also because one of the major weaknesses of the study is the biased sample. Participants in Milgram's study consisted of 40 males, all aged between 20-50 (Milgram, 1963). Due to the fact that all participants were white American citizens it would be interesting to implement study with participants all around the world, this may include different ethnicities, ages, genders and classes. This way it would be easier to generalize the study to the world population and see differences in actions if such will occur. We predict dramatic changes in attitudes over the years. We believe also that factors such as age and religion may influence people's behavior. Due to drastic changes in our society, this may also include politics factors, such as: development of democracy and human rights participants would not obeyed authority in the same way.

title_r: The religiosity as social value hypothesis: A multi-method replication and extension across 65 countries and three levels of spatial aggregation.
abstract_r: Are religious people psychologically better or worse adjusted than their nonreligious counterparts? Hundreds of studies have reported a positive relation between religiosity and psychological adjustment. Recently, however, a comparatively small number of cross-cultural studies has questioned this staple of religiosity research. The latter studies find that religious adjustment benefits are restricted to religious cultures. Gebauer, Sedikides, and Neberich (2012) suggested the religiosity as social value hypothesis (RASV) as one explanation for those cross-cultural differences. RASV states that, in religious cultures, religiosity possesses much social value, and, as such, religious people will feel particularly good about themselves. In secular cultures, however, religiosity possesses limited social value, and, as such, religious people will feel less good about themselves, if at all. Yet, previous evidence has been inconclusive regarding RASV and regarding cross-cultural differences in religious adjustment benefits more generally. To clarify matters, we conducted 3 replication studies. We examined the relation between religiosity and self-esteem (the most direct and appropriate adjustment indicator, according to RASV) in a self-report study across 65 countries (N = 2,195,301), an informant-report study across 36 countries (N = 560,264), and another self-report study across 1,932 urban areas from 243 federal states in 18 countries (N = 1,188,536). Moreover, we scrutinized our results against 7, previously untested, alternative explanations. Our results fully and firmly replicated and extended prior evidence for cross-cultural differences in religious adjustment benefits. These cross-cultural differences were best explained by RASV. title_r: Psychometric Reliability of ERN and Pe Across Flanker, Stroop, and Go/No-Go Tasks: A Direct and Conceptual Replication
abstract_r:
OSF registration template: Open-Ended Registration

The purpose of this study is to replicate and extend work on the psychometric reliability of cognitive control event-related potentials (ERPs) as a function of increasing trials across three different tasks (Meyer et al., 2013, Psychophysiology). Our primary aim is a direct replication of Meyer et al. (2013) to determine the number of trials needed for adequate psychometric internal consistency (.70) of the error-related negativity (ERN) recorded during flanker, Stroop, and Go/no-go tasks using classical test theory estimates (i.e., coefficient alpha). Our second aim is to extend these findings by conducting a conceptual replication examining generalizability theory estimates of internal consistency (i.e., dependability) of ERN, correct-response negativity (CRN), post-error positivity (Pe), post-correct positivity (Pc), and their difference scores (ERN, Pe; error minus correct) as a function of the number of trials across the three tasks. We will use post-estimation contrasts to identify task differences in dependability and ICC estimates as function of the number of trials recoded.

title_r: Extreme weather, climate change, climate action and uncertainty distress: A replication study using network analysis.
abstract_r: Both extreme weather and climate change have been linked to distress and at times mental health problems. Pro-environmental actions have often been related to higher distress. The uncertainty distress model (Freeston et al., 2020) proposes that in real-world situations, perceptions of threat and uncertainty contribute to distress. Freeston, Sermin-Read, et al. (2023) recruited a community sample (N = 327) who completed an online survey. Network analysis was used to analyse the relationships between the variables. Exposure to extreme weather, perceptions of climate change, climate change distress and pro-environmental action were measured along with symptoms of adjustment disorder and post-traumatic stress disorder, and uncertainty intolerance and behaviours. They reported there was variable exposure to extreme weather, but greater exposure was associated with more severe post-traumatic symptoms. Pro-environmental action was associated with greater severity of adjustment disorder symptoms. The perception that climate change was happening now was linked positively to pro-environmental action and negatively to perceptions of uncertainty about whether climate change was happening. The results replicated several findings from the emerging climate change distress literature and are consistent with some predictions of the uncertainty distress model, but not others. Aim: The main aim of the current study is to conduct a replication using network analysis with 1) improved measurement in some areas (see above and in measures section), 2) a larger and more diverse sample (see recruitment methods). The network analysis will follow the previous analysis as much as possible to facilitate comparison. Methods: The study will essentially replicate the previous study with the following modifications: inclusion of heatwaves; expand the type, timescale and impact of warnings; differentiated assessment of disruption; fuller range of emotional responses; shortened/improved versions of other measures. A larger sample will be sought, recruited to increase not only the diversity and representativeness of the sample, but also the geographical distribution and so the range of experiences of extreme weather. Results: Descriptive analyses of the participants, the experiences of extreme weather, and network analysis will be reported, based on the previous study.

title_r: Factor Structure And Affective Composition Of The Chills: Replication And Extension
abstract_r: “The chills” refers to a set of bodily sensations (goosebumps, tingling, coldness, and shivers) that sometimes accompany strong emotion (Maruskin, Thrash & Elliot, 2012). Past factor analyses of the chills identified a multi-factor, hierarchical structure, consisting of four lower-order factors (goosebumps, tingling, coldness, and shivers) and two higher-order factors (goosetingles and coldshivers). Research on the affective nomological nets of particular chills factors provided additional evidence of the discriminant validity of the two higher-order and the four-lower-order factors (Maruskin, Thrash & Elliot, 2012; Wadsworth, 2019). Despite evidence of discriminant validity, most researchers have continued to treat the chills as a unitary construct. The goal of the present study is to replicate and extend evidence that the chills consists of a set of distinguishable sensations with distinct affective correlates. Specifically, I aim to (a) replicate the factor structure of the chills and (b) further test whether the four lower-order sensations show distinct relations to core affect variables. Using the narrative recall method, the present study assessed chills sensations and core affect during recalled chills experience. Results of factor analyses replicated the factor structure of the chills established by Maruskin et al. (2012). Results of circumplex analyses provided additional evidence of the discriminant validity of higher-order and lower-order sensations. Goosetingles tended to accompany pleasant states, whereas coldshivers tended to accompany unpleasant states. Furthermore, relative to goosebumps, tingling accompanied states lower on activation and higher on pleasure. Relative to coldness, shivers accompanied states lower on displeasure and higher on activation. These findings are consistent with but refine the conclusions of Maruskin et al. (2012) and point to the value of incorporating the affect circumplex in understanding the chills.

title_r: Effects of the Generic Masculine and its Alternatives in Germanophone countries. A Multi-lab Replication and Extension of Stahlberg, Sczesny, and Braun, 2001
abstract_r: In languages such as German, French, or Hindi, plural forms of job occupations and societal roles are often in a generic-masculine form instead of a gender-neutral form. Although meant as “generic”, this generic-masculine form excludes women from everyday language and might even entail the cognitive effect that listeners and readers will less likely think of women. Several studies have demonstrated this and related cognitive effects in the past. Due to the societal relevance of gender-neutral language, we propose a direct replication and extension of a classic study by Stahlberg, Sczesny, and Braun (2001, Experiment 2) in a multi-lab setting. We already present preliminary evidence showing that people indeed come up with more female exemplars when they are asked to name celebrities from several domains, such as politics and sports in gender-neutral forms compared to the generic-masculine form. The proposed multi-lab study will be conducted among 12 labs, collecting data from more than N = 2,000 participants.

title_r: Not toeing the number line for simple arithmetic: Two large-n conceptual replications of Mathieu et al. (Cognition, 2016, Experiment 1)
abstract_r: We conducted two conceptual replications of Experiment 1 in Mathieu, Gourjon, Couderc, Thevenot, and Prado (2016, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cognition.2015.10.002). They tested a sample of 34 French adults on mixed-operation blocks of single-digit addition (4 + 3) and subtraction (4 – 3) with the three problem elements (O1, +/-, O2) presented sequentially. Addition was 34 ms faster if O2 appeared 300 ms after the operation sign and displaced 5° to the right of central fixation, whereas subtraction was 19 ms faster when O2 was displaced to the left. Replication Experiment 1 (n = 74 recruited at the University of Saskatchewan) used the same non-zero addition and subtraction problems and trial event sequence as Mathieu et al., but participants completed blocks of pure addition and pure subtraction followed by the mixed-operation condition used by Mathieu et al. Addition RT showed a 32 ms advantage with O2 shifted rightward relative to leftward but only in mixed-operation blocks. There was no effect of O2 position on subtraction RT. Experiment 2 (n = 74) was the same except mixed-operation blocks occurred before the pure-operation blocks. There was an overall 13 ms advantage with O2 shifted right relative to leftward but no interaction with operation or with mixture (i.e., pure vs mixed operations). Nonetheless, the rightward RT advantage was statistically significant for both addition and subtraction only in mixed-operation blocks. Taken together with the robust effects of mixture in Experiment 1, the results suggest that O2 position effects in this paradigm might reflect task specific demands associated with mixed operations.

title_r: Conceptual replication and extension of the relation between the number line estimation task and mathematical competence across seven studies
abstract_r: A recent meta-analysis demonstrated the overall correlation between the number line estimation (NLE) task and children’s mathematical competence was r = .44 (positively recoded), and this relation increased with age. The goal of the current study was to conceptually replicate and extend these results by further synthesizing this correlation utilizing studies not present in the meta-analysis. Across seven studies, 954 participants, ranging from 3 to 11 years old (Age M = 6.02 years, SD = 1.57), the overall estimation-competence correlations were similar to those of the meta-analysis and ranged from r = −.40 to −.35. The current conceptual replication demonstrated that the meta-analysis captured a stable overall relation between performance on the NLE task and mathematical competence. However, the current study failed to replicate the same moderation of age group presented in the meta-analysis. Furthermore, the current study extended results by assessing the stability and predictive validity of the NLE task while controlling for covariates. Results suggested that the NLE task demonstrated poor stability and predictive validity in the seven samples present in this study. Thus, although concurrent relations replicated, the differential age moderation, lack of stability, and lack of predictive validity in these studies require a more nuanced approach to understanding the utility of the NLE task. Future research should focus on understanding the connection between children’s developmental progression and NLE measurement before further investigating the predictive and diagnostic importance of the task for broader mathematical competence.

title_r: Contralateral delay activity as a marker of visual working memory capacity: a multi-site registered replication
abstract_r: Visual working memory (VWM) is a temporary storage system capable of retaining information that can be accessed and manipulated by higher cognitive processes, thereby facilitating a wide range of cognitive functions. Electroencephalography (EEG) is used to understand the neural correlates of VWM with high temporal precision, and one commonly used EEG measure is an event-related potential called the contralateral delay activity (CDA). In a landmark study by Vogel and Machizawa (2004), the authors found that the CDA amplitude increases with the number of items stored in VWM and plateaus around three to four items, which is thought to represent the typical adult working memory capacity. Critically, this study also showed that the increase in CDA amplitude between two-item and four-item arrays correlated with individual subjects’ VWM performance. Although these results have been supported by subsequent studies, a recent study suggested that the number of subjects used in experiments investigating the CDA may not be sufficient to detect differences in set size and to provide a reliable account of the relationship between behaviorally measured VWM capacity and the CDA amplitude. To address this, the current study, as part of the #EEGManyLabs project, aims to conduct a multi-site replication of Vogel and Machizawa's (2004) seminal study on a large sample of participants, with a pre-registered analysis plan. Through this, our goal is to contribute to deepening our understanding of the neural correlates of visual working memory.

title_r: How strong is the rhythm of perception? A registered replication of Hickok et al. (2015)
abstract_r: Our ability to predict upcoming events is a fundamental component of human cognition. One way in which we do so is by exploiting temporal regularities in sensory signals: the ticking of a clock, falling of footsteps and the motion of waves each provide a structure that may facilitate anticipation. But how strong is the effect of rhythmic anticipation on perception? And to what degree do people vary in their ability to capitalize on these regularities? In 2015, Hickok et al. introduced a behavioural paradigm to assess how a rhythmic auditory stimulus affects perception of subsequent targets (Hickok G, Farahbod H, Saberi K. 2015 The rhythm of perception: entrainment to acoustic rhythms induces subsequent perceptual oscillation. Psychol. Sci. 26, 1006–1013. (doi:10.1177/0956797615576533)). They tested five listeners and found that perception (target detection accuracy) fluctuated rhythmically just like the sound rhythm. Here, we replicate the original finding, assess how likely the finding is to be observed for any individual, and quantify effect size in a large sample of adult listeners (n = 149). We introduce a model-based analysis approach that allows separate estimates of amplitude and phase information in target detection responses, and quantifies effect size for individual listeners. Together our results strongly support the presence of oscillatory influences on target detection accuracy, as well as substantial variability in the magnitude of this effect across listeners.

title_r: Revisiting Self-Efficacy in Computer Science: A Replication Study
abstract_r: Self-efficacy is a reliable predictor of academic motivation and achievement across academic disciplines and age groups (Lishinski et al. 2016; Zimmerman et al. 1992). Because self-efficacy can be improved through instructional experiences and tools, identifying students with low self-efficacy or strategies to increase it is valuable in computing education. For this reason, measurements of self-efficacy are important for educators and researchers. The goal of the study is to replicate the findings from Steinhorst et al. (2020) validation study of their newly designed self-efficacy measurement for introductory programming students. Additionally, the intention is to extend the work by incorporating new measures of general (i.e., domain-independent) self-efficacy to assess convergent validity and explore measurements over time. Students completed several instruments related to general self-efficacy once at the beginning and programming self-efficacy at the beginning and end of the semester. Half of the current studys scales were used in the original study, so this population can be directly compared to the original populations. New scales for general self-efficacy were added to examine convergent validity and potential differences between general and programming-specific self-efficacy. The results revealed robust internal consistency and construct validity of the Steinhorst instrument for both the introductory programming course and the data structures course, aligning with the general self-efficacy theory. Additionally, the findings highlight the Steinhorst Instrument's suitability for different languages and contexts. A significant insight from the study is the necessity for researchers and educators to modify the instrument accordingly, ensuring that items not covered in the curriculum are excluded. This research enhances researchers' and educators' understanding of the Steinhorst instrument's robustness for assessing programming self-efficacy across various educational contexts.

title_r: “I Actually Eat That Much Meat”: Unsuccessful Replication of Women’s Situational Underreporting of Meat Consumption
abstract_r: Abstract When reminded of the suffering of animals on farms, men and women employ different strategies to justify their meat consumption. This pre-registered study aimed to conceptually replicate Rothgerber’s (2019) finding that women underreport their meat consumption to reduce meat-related cognitive dissonance. MTurk-workers ( N = 804) were subjected to a 2 (treatment: farm animal abuse salience vs. control) × 2 (gender: male vs. female) high-powered experimental design. Results suggest that neither men nor women in the farm animal abuse condition reported eating less meat overall – respectively less beef, pork, chicken, fish, or more vegetarian food – compared to the control condition. People high in Honesty-Humility reported less meat consumption independently from treatment group and gender. In conclusion, women may not use perceived behavioral change as a justification strategy more than men, or at all. Possible reasons for replication failure are discussed.

title_r: International adjustment of female vs male business expatriates. A replication study in Switzerland
abstract_r: Purpose - – Reasons for women’s underrepresentation in international assignments include stereotypical assumptions within organizations about their ability to adjust abroad and more broadly a lack of trust from the corporate headquarters. Female expatriates’ adjustment may strongly vary depending on the host country and on host-country nationals’ attitudes toward them. Yet up until today, very few studies have examined female expatriate adjustment in a single and non-Asian host country. The purpose of this paper is to address this gap by comparing the cross-cultural adjustment of male and female expatriates in Switzerland. Design/methodology/approach - – This study replicates Selmer and Leung’s (2003a) study design in order to compare adjustment of male and female expatriates working in multinational companies in the French-speaking part of Switzerland. Based on 152 valid questionnaires collected, the authors performed a multivariate analysis of covariance and further analyses of covariance to compare male and female expatriate adjustment. Findings - – The authors find that female expatriates have significantly higher interaction and work adjustment levels than their male counterparts, while no significant differences between men and women were observed in terms of general adjustment. These findings in a European context are consistent with those of Selmer and Leung in an Asian context. Originality/value - – Very few studies to date have examined the adjustment of female expatriates in a western host-country context, despite the fact that host-country cultural norms might strongly influence women’s experiences. The research brings new empirical evidence about cross-cultural adjustment of female and male expatriates in a western location. Contrary to persistent stereotypical assumptions, results emphasize again that women are able to adjust better or at least as well as their male counterparts.

title_r: An Extended Active Learning Approach to Multiverse Analysis ? Predictions of Latent Variables from Graph Theory Measures of the Human Connectome and Their Direct Replication
abstract_r: Multiverse analysis has been proposed as a powerful technique to disclose the large number of degrees of freedom in data preprocessing and analysis that strongly contribute to the current replication crisis in science. However, in the field of imaging neuroscience, where multidimensional, complex and noisy data are measured, multiverse analysis may be computationally infeasible. The number of possible forking paths given by different methodological decisions and analytical choices is immense. Recently, Dafflon et al. (2022) proposed an active learning approach as an alternative to exhaustively exploring all forking paths [1]. Here, we aimed to extend their active learning pipeline by integrating latent underlying variables which are not directly observable. The extension to latent outcomes is particularly valuable for computational psychiatry and neurocognitive psychology, where latent traits are conceptualized as common cause of a variety of observable neural and behavioral symptoms. To illustrate our approach and to test its direct replicability, we analyzed the individual organization and topology of functional brain networks of two relatively large samples from the ABCD study dataset (N = 1491) and HCP dataset (N = 833). Graph-theoretical parameters that take into account both brain-wide and region-specific network properties were used as predictors of a latent variable reflecting general cognition [2]. Our results demonstrate the ability of the extended method to selectively explore the multiverse when predicting a latent variable. First, the low-dimensional space created with the proposed approach was able to cluster the forking paths according to their similarity. Second, the active learning approach successfully estimated the prediction performance of all pipelines in both datasets. To interactively explore the multiverse of results, we developed a Shiny app [ https://meteor-oldenburg.shinyapps.io/ExtendedAL/] to visualize the predictive accuracy resulting from each forking path and to illustrate the similarity between pipelines created by different combinations of data processing choice. The code for active learning and the app are available at [https://github.com/kristantodan12/ExtendedAL]

title_r: Market Access and Quality Upgrading: Evidence from Four Field Experiments. A Replication Study of Bold et al. (American Economic Review, 2022)
abstract_r: Bold et al. (2022) investigate the effect of providing access to a larger, centralized market where quality is rewarded with a premium on farm productivity and framing incomes from smallholder maize farmers in western Uganda, using a series of randomized experiments and a difference-in-differences approach. We successfully reproduce the results of this study using the publicly provided replication packet. Then test the robustness of these results by re-defining treatment and outcome variables, testing for model misspecification and the leverage of outliers, and testing for non-random selection in the Fisher-permutation process. Our results show that the findings in Bold et al. (2022) are robust to a variety of decisions in the research process. This evokes confidence in the internal validity of the findings.

title_r: Migration, Diversity, and Economic Growth. A Replication Study of Bove and Elia (World Development, 2017)
abstract_r: A recent and well known paper, Bove and Elia (2017), argues that migrants' diversity, as captured by the indexes of both fractionalization and polarization, exerts a positive effect on GDP growth. In fact, by using the same dataset and methodology, we show that the impact of diversity cannot be distinguished from that of migration itself due to the very high correlation among the corresponding variables. Also, if one disentangles migration from diversity, following Alesina et al. (2016), only migration maintains a positive impact on growth while diversity, as captured by fractionalization, turns out to be weakly and positively associated with growth, but limitedly to the 1980-2010 time span. Polarization, on the other hand, does not seem to exert any effect on growth. The question as to whether diversity is more or less beneficial in terms of economic growth remains therefore an intriguing one, and calls for more theoretical and empirical analyses, possibly based on less (geographically) aggregated data.

title_r: Meta-analysis and publication bias: How well does the FAT-PET-PEESE procedure work? A replication study of Alinaghi & Reed (Research Synthesis Methods, 2018)
abstract_r: This R-code produces the results of the replication study. Abstract of the paper: A meta-analysis is a tool for aggregating estimates of a similar “effect” across many studies. Publication bias is the phenomenon where literature is sample selected in favor of studies having statistically significant results and/or having estimates that satisfy pre-conceived expectations. A popular procedure used for conducting meta-analyses in the presence of publication bias is the FAT-PET-PEESE (FPP) procedure. In a recent paper published in \emph{Research Synthesis Methods}, Alinaghi and Reed (2018), utilizing Monte Carlo simulations, report that the FPP procedure does not work well when used in “realistic” data environments where true effects differ both across and within studies. AR’s findings are important because the FPP approach is dominant in the economics meta-analysis literature. I replicate their results and discover two mistakes, which I subsequently correct. The first mistake is found in a descriptive statistics table, misrepresenting the overview of simulated dataset. The second is associated with the fixed effect estimation, generating erroneous estimated effects and Type I error. Further, I extend their analysis by making their simulation environment even more realistic. Despite producing somewhat different results, my replications generally confirm AR’s conclusions about the unreliability of the FPP procedure in realistic data environments.

title_r: Does text generation improve learning from expository text? A conceptual replication attempt
abstract_r: The aim of the present study was to test the replicability of the text generation effect for learning with expository texts while systematically varying contextual factors that—based on extant literature—can be assumed to affect the occurrence and magnitude of the text generation effect. Seven experiments were conducted in which participants either read (control condition) or unscrambled sentences (generation condition) in expository texts. The experiments varied systematically on intentionality of learning, learning time constraint, retention interval, and study design. Contrary to expectations, no text generation effect could be found. Instead, some of the experiments even revealed a learning disadvantage for text generation compared to the reading control condition. In only one experiment (Experiment 6) and for just one of the learning measures, learners performed better when they had generated the texts. In sum, the results indicate that a generation effect is most likely to occur when learning is intentional, when learning time is unrestricted, and for immediate testing. The findings suggest that the applications of text generation in educational contexts are rather limited.

title_r: Lexical prediction in language comprehension: a replication study of grammatical gender effects in Dutch
abstract_r: An important question in predictive language processing is the extent to which prediction effects can reliably be measured on pre-nominal material (e.g., articles before nouns). Here, we present a large sample (N=58) close replication of a study by Otten and van Berkum [2009, Does working memory capacity affect the ability to predict upcoming words in discourse? Brain Research, 1291, 92–101. doi: 10.1016/j.brainres.2009.07.042]. They report ERP modulations in relation to the predictability of nouns in sentences, measured on gender-marked Dutch articles. We used nearly identical materials, procedures, and data analysis steps. We fail to replicate the original effect, but do observe a pattern consistent with the original data. Methodological differences between our replication and the original study that could potentially have contribute to the diverging results are discussed. In addition, we discuss the suitability of Dutch gender-marked determiners as a test-case for future studies of pre-activation of lexical items.

title_r: The Incremental Validity of Average States: A Replication and Extension of Finnigan & Vazire (2018)
abstract_r: States refer to our momentary thoughts, feelings, and behaviors. Average states (aggregates across multiple time points) are discussed as a more accurate and objective measure of personality compared to global self-reports since they do not only rely on people’s general beliefs about themselves. Specifically, Finnigan and Vazire (2018) argued that, if average states better capture what a person is actually like, this should be reflected in their unique association with informant-reports of personality, and tested this idea based on two experience-sampling studies. Their results showed, however, that average self-reported states did not predict global informant-reported personality above and beyond global self-reports. In this research, we aimed at replicating and extending these results. We used data of five studies (total N = 806) that involved global self- and informant reports and employed a variety of different experience-sampling methods (time-based with different sampling schedules, event-based). Across all studies, the original results (i.e., no incremental effects of average self-reported states) were replicated. Furthermore, as an extension to the original study, we found that average other-reported states (provided by peers, results based on one study) did indeed predict global informant-reports above and beyond global self-reports. These findings highlight the importance of differentiating between method effects (global reports vs average states) from source of information effects (self vs. other). We discuss these results, focusing on the suitability of using informant-reports as a criterion variable and conceptual differences between assessment methods.

title_r: Sex Differences in Mate Preferences Across 45 Cultures: A Large-Scale Replication
abstract_r:
OSF registration template: Open-Ended Registration

summary: Pre-registration: Sex Differences in Mate Preferences Across 45 Cultures: A Large-Scale Replication

Kathryn V. Walter & Daniel Conroy-Beam

Department of Psychological and Brain Sciences, University of California, Santa Barbara 

Date pre-registered on the Open Science Framework: April 17, 2018
This document was fixed in its current form prior to data analysis, all later amendments will be visible.

Date Made Public: April 17, 2021

Correspondence regarding this pre-registration should be addressed to Kathryn V. Walter, Email: kathryn.walter@psych.ucsb.edu, or using the comment function on the Open Science Framework. 
Pre-registration: Sex Differences in Mate Preferences Across 45 Cultures: A Large-Scale Replication
This study will attempt to replicate classic cross-cultural findings from the human mating literature. Specifically, we will examine sex differences in mate preferences across cultures (Buss, 1989); the multivariate effect size of these differences (Conroy-Beam et al., 2015); sex differences in the age of chosen long-term partners (Kenrick & Keefe, 1992; Buss, 1989), cross-cultural variability in mate preferences as a function of pathogen prevalence (Gangestad & Buss, 1993; Gangestad, Haselton & Buss, 2006), and cross-cultural variability in sex differences in mate preferences as a function of gender equality (Eagly & Wood, 1999; Gangestad, Haselton & Buss, 2006; Zentner & Mitura, 2012). 
Method
Participants
Data has already been collected, in person (not online), from participants in 45 different countries, n = 14,487 (7,961 female). Each study site collected data from both university populations and community samples. Due to a lack of records from about half of the sites, there is incomplete information about the percentage of each type of sample. From the sites that did keep records (n = 6,637), 47.14% (n = 3,129) came from community samples. Age of participants ranged from 18-91 years old (Mdn = 25, M = 28.79, SD = 10.64). Of the total sample, most participants reported being in ongoing, committed relationships (n = 9,236, 63.75%). 
Exclusion criteria. If data is unavailable for certain countries for the various indices used, those countries will not be included in those specific analyses (we will note in the paper which countries have been excluded due to lack of available data). Participants who were under the age of 18 when taking the survey were excluded from the sample. Participants who did not fill out any part of the mate preferences survey or did not report their sex were excluded from the sample as well. Two countries surveyed did not include the mate preferences portion of the survey (Serbia and Ukraine) and will not be included in analyses. 
Measures
Mate preferences. Participants completed a 5-item questionnaire on ideal mate preferences for a long-term romantic partner. Participants rated their ideal romantic partner on five traits: kindness, intelligence, health, physical attractiveness, and good financial prospects. All items were rated on bipolar adjective scales ranging from 1 (e.g. very unintelligent) to 7 (e.g. very intelligent).
Age. Participants reported their own age in years as part of a demographic questionnaire. Participants in relationships additionally reported the age of their actual long-term romantic partner. 
Pathogen prevalence. We will use a variety of measures of pathogen prevalence from the prior literature and from publicly available databases. These include the pathogen prevalence index developed by Low (1990) and used in Gangestad & Buss (1993); years of life lost to communicable diseases (Debruine et al., 2010); and years of life lost to infectious and parasitic diseases (WHO, 2015) and estimated deaths due to infectious and parasitic diseases (WHO, 2015). For the variables from publicly available databases, we collected the most recent available data in all cases.
Gender equality. We will use a variety of measures of gender equality from the prior literature and publicly available databases. We will use the Gender Development Index (GDI) and Gender Empowerment Measure (GEM) from Eagly and Wood (1999). We will additionally use updated gender equality measures including the Global Gender Gap Index (GGGI) (World Economic Forum, 2016), the Gender Inequality Index (GII) (United Nations Development Programme, 2015), and the updated version of the GDI (United Nations Development Programme, 2015). For the publicly available databases, we collected the most recent available data for all variables.
Control variables. We will include a series of four control variables.  These control variables will be GDP per capita (CIA World Factbook), latitude (CIA World Factbook), most common religion (CIA World Factbook), and world region (based on Gangestad, Haselton, & Buss, 2006). 
Analysis Plan
We will conduct all primary analyses using multilevel models. In these models, participants will be nested within countries. When possible, the models will include all random effects for both slopes and intercepts. Should we experience convergence issues with these models, we will have to adjust model parameters in an exploratory fashion (e.g. dropping random slope terms) and we will report our decisions clearly. Multilevel models provide several advantages over traditional approaches for analyzing this kind of cross-cultural data. These models will allow us to estimate sex differences in mate preferences overall in the data, as well as the variability in these sex differences across cultures based on the random effects. Department of Psychological and Brain Sciences, University of California, Santa Barbara
